newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Inchcape clears decks for expansion.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Inchcape clears decks for expansion.

text.p: Inchcape Plc announced a 12 percent rise in headline profits on Monday and said it would now be investing for expansion, to fill the gap left by last year's clear-out of non-core businesses.
The multinational car dealer to soft drinks bottler reported a pretax profit of 165.1 million pounds ($264.7 million) before exceptional items, compared with 146.8 million pounds in 1995.
A bright outlook for 1997 reassured investors and the share price was up 11 pence to 266-1/2p in a generally weak market after the news.
"The key thing...was positive comments on prospects for growth," said Andrew Ripper, a London-based analyst at Merrill Lynch.

Chairman Sir Colin Marshall said trading in the remaining businesses was expected to improve this year, although first-half results would show a big gap left by the sale of Bain Hogg insurance business, which now had to be filled.
"But we have got the company into a good position," he told Reuters. "We are confident of improvement from our continuing businesses."

Operating profits came in at 195 million pounds against 119.9 million pounds last time, on marginally lower sales of 6.26 billion pounds, and the total dividend was raised five percent to 10.5 pence a share.

Group pretax profits after exceptionals and interest jumped to 107 million pounds from 17.4 million pounds in 1995 but results were distorted by the sale of its Bain Hogg insurance and Testing Services businesses for a total of 540 million pounds.
The sale of Bain Hogg and Testing Services helped wipe out net debt of 463 million pounds a year ago to leave the group with net cash of 39.9 million pounds at the end of 1996.

"We have a strong balance sheet," Marshall said. "We are going to take our position cautiously as we go forward but we will look at opportunities for expanding what we already have and adding to it," he said. The company wants to expand its car dealing businesses as well as develop its soft drinks operations, he said. Last year operating profits at the Motors division increased 29 percent to 126.6 million pounds, helped by a strong performance from its Toyota franchises. The company said the performance of its products marketing services businesses, which operate in the Asia-Pacific and Middle East, were "disappointing", with profits falling seven percent to 30.2 million pounds, but the operation has now been reorganised. The business was split in December into two regional groups, based in Singapore and Dubai and it was announced on Monday that Singapore-listed affiliate Inchcape Berhad is to demerge the marketing services from its vehicle operations.

Meanwhile operating profits in the soft drinks bottling business which has concentrated on developing new overseas markets for Coca-Cola Co, fell to 8.2 million pounds last year from 13 million in 1995, despite sales doubling to 197.8 million pounds. Inchcape said strong profits in Chile "were offset by substantial start-up losses in Russia, as expected, and by weakness in the Peruvian soft drinks market." But Inchcape chief executive Philip Cushing told a news conference that the firm was increasing its market share in Peru and expects to have its new Russian business out of the red by 1998.

The company announced on Monday that its Peruvian unit Embotelladora Latinoamericana SA (ELSA) had added to its repertoire by buying the San Luis mineral water and Kola Inglesa brands, for 25 million pounds, an example of its new acquisitive strategy.

"It was only 25 million pounds but there are plenty of other opportunities to add to that business," Cushing said. Inchcape also plans to open its third and fourth Coca-Cola bottling plants in Russia later this year.
Cushing said the plants have taken longer than expected and cost more than elsewhere to build, but all four would be running by September, serving six Coca-Cola franchises across Russia.
"By the end of 1997 we will have the network in place and then the thing will really start to hum," Cushing said.
